title: Beyond Accuracy: Explainable Analysis of Weather and Lighting Recognition for Autonomous Driving
content: Autonomous vehicles (AVs) must recognize weather and lighting conditions that affect perception and driving decisions. Classification accuracy alone, however, does not reveal which visual evidence a model uses. We apply explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) to condition recognition on 31,420 CARLA images spanning 21 weather–time classes. ResNet18 and ResNet50 are compared with global color baselines, and Grad-CAM and Integrated Gradients (IG) explain predictions from a designated ResNet18 model. Across three training seeds, the neural models achieve internal joint accuracies of 99.547 ± 0.123% and 99.710 ± 0.117%, respectively (mean ± sample standard deviation), with detected structural-similarity groups kept within partitions. Analysis of 210 correct and all 18 incorrect predictions reveals masking sensitivity to replacement choices and prediction correctness. After full parameter randomization, signed IG correlations approach zero while positive-grid correlations remain around 0.4, showing that different attribution representations can yield different assessments. These findings demonstrate how explanatory analysis complements accuracy in evaluating AV perception models, while independent-route generalization remains unverified. Future work will extend the analysis from simulation to real driving images using the Adverse Conditions Dataset with Correspondences (ACDC), with compatible tasks for comparing explanations across domains. This simulation-to-real extension aims to inform the development of explanation-aware AV benchmarks that evaluate predictive performance alongside explanation robustness.
